planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Old Lady Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Old Lady Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. A rounded, clustering cactus densely covered in long, fine, white hairs that give it a soft, shaggy, almost fur-covered appearance among sharp little spines, it produces a ring of small, bright pink to magenta flowers around the crown in spring, a cheerful contrast to its snowy-white body. Native to central Mexico, it is a popular, easy-care species for a sunny windowsill or outdoor xeriscape container, clustering readily with age into an attractive mounded colony of multiple heads. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light for the fullest hair coverage, and protect from frost and prolonged cold, damp conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Powder Puff Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Powder Puff Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. Small, rounded stems are densely covered in soft, fine, silky white hairs interspersed with a few longer, hooked golden spines, giving the clustering colony a fluffy, cotton-ball-like texture, topped with small creamy-yellow to pale pink flowers in spring. Native to central Mexico, it offsets freely and quickly forms a dense mound of dozens of small heads, making it one of the faster-clustering and most crowd-pleasing miniature cacti for a sunny windowsill dish garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light for the best hair density, and separate offsets to propagate or share.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; peanut cactus is one of the easiest flowering cacti, tolerating some neglect and irregular watering.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; peanut cactus is one of the easiest flowering cacti, tolerating some neglect and irregular watering. Slender, finger-like, pale green stems covered in soft white spines sprawl and branch loosely, forming a low, spreading clump that resembles a pile of small peanuts, and it rewards even minimal care with a generous flush of large, brilliant orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring that dwarf the small stems bearing them. Native to Argentina, it is easy to grow and propagate, readily forming offsets that root wherever a stem segment touches soil, making it a favorite beginner cactus for a bright windowsill or hanging basket. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide plenty of direct sun for the best flowering, and separate rooted offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Easter Lily Cactus needs excellent drainage and blooms most reliably with strong light and a distinct winter rest.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Easter Lily Cactus needs excellent drainage and blooms most reliably with strong light and a distinct winter rest. A nearly spineless, softly ribbed, rounded pale green globe produces enormous, pure white, intensely fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers that open at dusk and last only a day or two, but are so large relative to the small plant body that a single bloom can seem to dwarf the cactus itself. Native to Bolivia and Argentina, it clusters readily by producing offset pups around the base of the mother plant, and its lack of significant spines makes it easier to handle than most globe cacti. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light and a cooler, drier winter rest to encourage the following season's flowers, and separate offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Red Crown Cactus flowers most reliably when given a cool, dry winter rest followed by increased water and light in spring.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Red Crown Cactus flowers most reliably when given a cool, dry winter rest followed by increased water and light in spring. Small, flattened, globular stems covered in short, fine spines cluster readily at the base into a low mat, and in spring the plant produces a ring of brilliant orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers encircling the crown, disproportionately large and vivid for such a small cactus body. Native to high-elevation grasslands in Bolivia and Argentina, it is one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the small globular cacti, often blooming as a very young plant and continuing for years with minimal care. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide a distinct cooler, drier winter rest to trigger the next season's bloom, and separate offsets to propagate a colony.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the green species form tolerates more direct sun, while the brightly colored grafted forms sold as 'moon cactus' need protection from intense direct sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the green species form tolerates more direct sun, while the brightly colored grafted forms sold as 'moon cactus' need protection from intense direct sun. In its natural green form this small, rounded, ribbed cactus from Paraguay and Brazil bears attractive pale pink to white flowers, but it is far better known in cultivation for its chlorophyll-free color mutants — brilliant red, orange, yellow, or pink globes — which lack the green pigment needed to photosynthesize and are grafted as small caps atop a green Hylocereus or Selenicereus cactus rootstock to survive. These colorful grafted 'moon cactus' combinations are common, inexpensive houseplants but are ultimately temporary, since the graft union eventually fails after a few years even with good care, at which point the colorful top can sometimes be re-grafted onto fresh rootstock. Water sparingly, avoid direct hot sun which can scorch the color mutant tops, and expect the brightly colored forms to need eventual regrafting rather than indefinite growth on their own roots.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Golden Ball Cactus is more tolerant of light shade than many columnar cacti but colors and flowers best in full sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Golden Ball Cactus is more tolerant of light shade than many columnar cacti but colors and flowers best in full sun. A densely ribbed, cylindrical cactus is entirely clothed in soft, glowing golden-yellow spines that catch the light and give the whole plant a warm, luminous glow, starting as a rounded ball and slowly elongating into a short column over many years, eventually producing bright yellow flowers near the crown once mature. Native to southern Brazil, it is slow-growing but very long-lived and low-maintenance, tolerating a wide range of indoor and outdoor conditions better than many spinier, more temperamental cacti. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much direct light as possible for the richest golden spine color, and protect from frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Silver Torch Cactus is one of the more cold-tolerant columnar cacti, handling brief light frost once mature, but still needs sharp drainage.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Silver Torch Cactus is one of the more cold-tolerant columnar cacti, handling brief light frost once mature, but still needs sharp drainage. Tall, slender, upright columns are densely covered in fine, silvery-white spines and bristles that give the whole plant a soft, shimmering, silvery glow, eventually clustering into a dramatic grove of columns from a single base as the plant ages over many years. Native to high-elevation slopes in Bolivia and Argentina, it produces striking, deep magenta-red tubular flowers along its upper sides once mature enough, though the silvery, architectural form is the main draw for most growers long before flowering size is reached. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much direct sun as possible for the densest, whitest spine coverage, and protect young plants from hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; bunny ears cactus is spineless but covered in fine, easily detached glochids that irritate skin, so handle with thick gloves or folded paper.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; bunny ears cactus is spineless but covered in fine, easily detached glochids that irritate skin, so handle with thick gloves or folded paper. Flattened, rounded, pale green pads studded with regularly spaced tufts of tiny golden-yellow glochids give the plant a charming polka-dot pattern, and new pads branch off in pairs from the top of older ones, loosely resembling a bunny's ears as the plant matures into a many-padded clump. Despite lacking true spines, the fine, barbed glochids detach at the slightest touch and embed painfully in skin, so this cactus is best displayed out of reach of curious hands, pets, and passing foot traffic. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide full sun for compact, well-spaced pad growth, and remove and root fallen pads to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
